summary: Learners build the pH scale as a 0–14 continuum (acids below 7, pure water neutral at 7 at 25 °C, alkalis above 7) by testing real or simulated substances with indicators and watching pH move during neutralisation. The KS3 meaning of acid/alkali is developed through neutralisation (an acid and alkali cancel toward 7); the hydrogen-ion (H+) concentration account and the strength-vs-concentration distinction are deepened at KS4. Core activities: a testing bench that maps indicator colour to pH for everyday substances, a mixing/titration task that drives pH through 7 at neutralisation, and reference/sequencing/categorisation support. An extension activity targets the persistent strength-vs-concentration misconception.
misconceptions: Neutral means 'no pH' or no reading rather than exactly 7.
A higher pH is always more dangerous / pH measures hazard rather than acidity.
All acids are strong and corrosive (ignoring weak/dilute acids like citric).
An alkali is just 'the opposite of dangerous', not itself potentially corrosive.
Adding more acid to an already acidic solution changes its identity rather than its concentration.

activities.title: Indicator testing bench: read pH from colour
steps: Add universal indicator to a set of everyday substances (e.g. lemon juice, vinegar, pure water, soap solution) and observe the colour each produces; corrosive substances such as oven cleaner should be shown only by teacher demonstration or simulation.
Map each colour onto a 0–14 pH strip: red-orange for low pH, green at 7, blue/purple for high pH.
Place each substance on the scale from the colour evidence, and label it acid, neutral, or alkali.
Also test with litmus as a two-way check: red indicates acidic, blue indicates alkaline.
State a rule connecting indicator colour to position on the pH scale.
activities.insight: Indicators make acidity visible: universal indicator gives a colour that maps to a specific pH, while litmus gives a two-way acid/alkali test. The pH scale is a continuum with neutral as the precise point 7, not an absence of reading.

activities.title: Neutralisation mixer: watch pH move toward 7
steps: Start with a strongly acidic solution that reads red (low pH) on indicator and meter.
Add alkali in small steps (drop by drop near neutral, where the pH changes very quickly) and watch the pH climb and the indicator colour change through orange and yellow to green around neutral (7).
Keep adding alkali past neutral and observe the colour continue into blue then purple as the solution becomes alkaline.
Describe in your own words what neutralisation means: an acid and an alkali cancel toward pH 7.
Predict, before each addition, which way the pH and colour will move; check against what you observe.
activities.insight: Mixing an acid with an alkali moves the pH toward 7 — they react and cancel rather than simply coexist. For a strong acid and strong alkali, neutral (7) is a precise crossing point; adding more alkali beyond it turns the solution alkaline, showing that neutral is a point on the scale you can pass, not an end point where nothing more can change.

activities.title: pH reference scale and sorting practice
steps: Use a colour-coded 0–14 pH reference with everyday substances pinned at their pH and an indicator-colour key; tap or point to a substance to recall its place.
Sequence a set of substances from lowest to highest pH.
Match indicator colours to their pH values.
Categorise substances as acid, neutral, or alkali.
Given a target such as 'set the pH to 7', identify a substance or mixture that would read there.
activities.insight: Consolidate the scale: ordering by pH, mapping colour to value, and sorting acid/neutral/alkali fix the continuum and the role of indicators as a reference for later testing.

activities.title: Strength vs concentration: predict, observe, explain
steps: Consider two bottles: very concentrated citric acid (the acid in lemons) and dilute hydrochloric acid.

Predict and explain your reasoning BEFORE testing, focusing on the difference between strength and concentration — note that which bottle is more corrosive (or reads lower pH) depends on the actual concentrations and cannot be settled by 'more concentrated' alone.

To get a determinate comparison, test equal-concentration solutions of citric and hydrochloric acid with universal indicator or a pH probe, and predict which reads the lower pH and why, before testing.
Observe the readings and compare them to your prediction.
Explain the result by separating how MUCH acid is dissolved (concentration) from how readily the acid releases hydrogen ions, H+ (strength).
activities.insight: Strength and concentration are different: strength is how fully an acid releases H+ ions (a property of the acid — hydrochloric is strong, citric is weak), while concentration is how much acid is dissolved and can be changed by dilution. At matched concentration the strong acid reads the lower pH; more broadly, corrosiveness depends on both strength and concentration, so a concentrated weak acid is not automatically more dangerous than a dilute strong one. Weak acids like citric and acetic are safe to eat at the low concentrations found in food, although concentrated forms can still be corrosive.

checkQuestion: I have a bottle of very concentrated citric acid (the acid in lemons) and a bottle of dilute hydrochloric acid. A student says 'the citric one must be more dangerous because it's more concentrated.' Which is likely to be the stronger, more corrosive acid — and the important part, explain the difference between how CONCENTRATED an acid is and how STRONG it is.
checkAnswer: The dilute hydrochloric acid can still be the more hazardous because STRENGTH and CONCENTRATION are different things. Strength is how fully the acid releases hydrogen ions (H⁺) — hydrochloric is a strong acid, citric is weak. Concentration is how much acid is dissolved in the water. A concentrated weak acid can be less corrosive than a dilute strong one. Full marks separate 'how much acid' (concentration) from 'how readily it gives H⁺ ions' (strength).
